children.text: Imagine a medical technology that works brilliantly for some patients but delivers systematically inferior results for others — not because of differences in the patients' underlying biology, but because the technology was built using data that did not include people like them. This is not a hypothetical. It is the current state of precision medicine.

The power of precision medicine comes from comparison: we understand whether a genetic variant is disease-causing by comparing its frequency in affected versus unaffected individuals, and by observing what happens to people who carry it. But if almost all the people in those comparisons share a similar ancestry, the insights generated are primarily valid for people of that ancestry.
The GWAS Diversity Problem: A Scientific Crisis, Not Just an Ethical One

A genome-wide association study (GWAS) is a research approach that scans the entire genome of thousands of people to find genetic variants that are statistically associated with a trait or disease. GWAS has identified tens of thousands of genetic associations across hundreds of conditions. But more than 90% of participants in published GWAS studies have been of European ancestry, even though people of European ancestry make up only about 16% of the world's population.

Why does this matter scientifically? Genetic associations found in European populations do not always replicate in other ancestry groups. The specific variants tagged in a GWAS study may differ by ancestry because linkage disequilibrium patterns — the way genetic variants are inherited together — vary between populations. A variant that reliably tags a disease-causing mutation in a European population may not tag the same mutation in an African or Asian population.

African-ancestry populations also have greater genetic diversity than European populations — a consequence of modern human populations originating in Africa and experiencing thousands of additional generations of evolution there before migrating to other continents. This means that studies restricted to European ancestry samples are sampling a genetically less diverse slice of humanity, potentially missing variants and associations that only exist in higher frequency in African or other non-European populations.

body.analogy: Imagine you want to build a highly accurate autocorrect algorithm for English. You train it almost exclusively on text written in British English — newspapers, novels, government documents. The algorithm works well for British English speakers. But when Australian, Nigerian, or Jamaican English speakers use it, it keeps flagging their perfectly correct words as mistakes, because those word patterns were absent from the training data. The algorithm is not wrong, exactly — it is just incomplete in a way that systematically disadvantages non-British users.
body.bridge: Genomic databases trained predominantly on European ancestry populations make better predictions for European ancestry individuals. For African, Indigenous, South Asian, and other non-European ancestry individuals, the predictions are less accurate — and clinical decisions based on those predictions are therefore less reliable.
body.concept: Why GWAS diversity matters for scientific validity

children.text: Polygenic Risk Scores: When the Training Data Is Not Diverse

A polygenic risk score (PRS) is a number calculated by summing up the small effects of hundreds or thousands of genetic variants to estimate a person's inherited risk for a complex trait or disease. PRS for conditions like coronary artery disease, type 2 diabetes, and breast cancer are moving toward clinical use. But PRS accuracy is strongly ancestry-dependent: a PRS trained on European data performs poorly when applied to individuals of African or Asian ancestry.

A 2019 study in Nature Genetics (Martin et al.) found that polygenic scores built from predominantly European data predicted risk about 4.5 times more accurately for people of European ancestry than for people of African ancestry, who are genetically farthest from the training population. Using a PRS with known poor accuracy for a patient of African ancestry without disclosing this limitation is a form of health inequity embedded in the technology itself.

If a cardiologist uses a coronary artery disease PRS to decide whether to intensify preventive treatment, and that PRS was trained entirely on European ancestry data, she is making decisions based on a risk estimate that is less accurate for her Black or South Asian patients than for her white patients. This is a clinical accuracy problem — and one that many providers do not know to ask about.
Algorithmic Bias in Genomic Interpretation Tools

The GWAS diversity gap has a direct clinical consequence: variant classification databases — the tools laboratories use to determine whether a genetic variant is pathogenic or benign — are also skewed toward European ancestry populations. When a clinical genetics lab identifies a variant in a patient of African ancestry, they look it up in databases like ClinVar. If that variant has only been observed in European populations before, it may be classified as a VUS (variant of uncertain significance) even if its clinical significance is actually well-established in other contexts.

This produces a systematic disparity in BRCA testing outcomes. Multiple studies have found that Black women receive VUS results from BRCA testing at substantially higher rates than white women — not because Black women's BRCA variants are intrinsically more ambiguous, but because there is less reference data from individuals of African ancestry in the databases used to classify variants. The result is diagnostic uncertainty that falls disproportionately on the patients who already face the most barriers to cancer care.

body.misconception: If a genetic test result comes back 'uncertain,' that reflects something ambiguous about the patient's biology.
body.reality: VUS findings often reflect gaps in the reference database, not ambiguity in the patient's biology. The same variant may be reclassified as benign or pathogenic as more data is added — especially data from underrepresented ancestries. Higher VUS rates in non-European patients are a measure of database inadequacy, not biological complexity.

children.text: The Economic Access Barrier: Who Can Actually Get Precision Medicine

Even if the genomic databases were fully equitable, precision medicine therapies face another equity barrier: cost. Many targeted cancer therapies, gene therapies, and genomic testing services are extraordinarily expensive — and coverage by Medicaid, the insurance program for low-income Americans, is inconsistent.

Consider Zolgensma, the gene therapy for spinal muscular atrophy discussed in Module 5. At approximately $2.1 million for a single infusion, it is one of the most expensive drugs ever approved. While manufacturers have patient assistance programs, access for Medicaid-enrolled patients has been inconsistent across states, and disparities in newborn screening follow-up — needed to identify eligible infants — have been documented along racial and socioeconomic lines.

Genetic counseling services face a similar access problem. There is a national shortage of genetic counselors — approximately 6,000 board-certified genetic counselors serve the entire United States, compared with over 300,000 primary care physicians. They are concentrated in urban academic medical centers. Rural patients, low-income patients without transportation, and patients who need counseling in languages other than English face significant barriers to accessing services that are increasingly central to precision medicine care.

children.text: Direct-to-Consumer Genomics: Promise vs. Reality for Low-Income Patients

Companies like 23andMe and AncestryDNA have made genetic testing accessible to millions of Americans at a price point of $100-300. In theory, this democratizes genomics. In practice, the equity picture is more complicated.

DTC tests are research-grade, not clinical-grade. They use genotyping arrays that detect a fixed set of known variants, not the comprehensive sequencing used in clinical laboratories. Health reports from DTC companies have documented accuracy limitations, particularly for non-European ancestry individuals, and the regulatory oversight of health claims is lighter than for clinical tests. A person who receives a DTC 'low risk for BRCA' result may have a false sense of reassurance if they carry a pathogenic variant the DTC array does not detect.

Furthermore, DTC genomic results require health literacy and access to clinical follow-up to be actionable. A low-income patient without a primary care provider who receives a 23andMe report showing elevated Alzheimer's or cancer risk faces the result without clinical support. For patients who have the least access to care, DTC genomics may create anxiety and confusion more often than clinical benefit.
NIH All of Us: Building the Diverse Biobank Precision Medicine Requires

The NIH All of Us Research Program, launched in 2018, is a national effort to build a biobank of 1 million or more diverse U.S. participants. The program explicitly prioritizes recruitment of communities that have historically been underrepresented in biomedical research: racial and ethnic minorities, rural residents, sexual and gender minorities, people with disabilities, and those without a college education. Participants donate health data, biological samples, and electronic health record access; in return, they receive their own genetic results.

As of 2025, All of Us had enrolled over 800,000 participants, with approximately 50% from racial or ethnic minority groups — a dramatic improvement over prior NIH biobank initiatives. The program has made its data available to approved researchers through a secure cloud-based platform, with the goal of generating genomic insights that are valid and actionable across the full diversity of the American population.

body.body: Vermont has been an active participant in the All of Us program, with enrollment sites at the University of Vermont Medical Center and community health centers across the state. The program's emphasis on rural participants — one of the most underrepresented groups in prior genomic research — has made Vermont an important recruiting ground. Vermont participants include residents from the Northeast Kingdom and other rural regions who would rarely have access to academic genomic research programs.
body.outcome: Vermont's All of Us enrollment has contributed to the program's goal of including rural Americans as a distinct population of interest, generating data relevant to understanding how geography, environmental exposures, and rural social determinants interact with genomic risk factors.
body.source: NIH All of Us Research Program, Vermont Enrollment Reports, 2024
body.title: NIH All of Us Research Program in Vermont

children.text: Historical Trauma and the Research Trust Deficit

Recruitment of underrepresented communities into genomic research cannot be separated from the history of exploitation in biomedical research. That history is not ancient — it extends into living memory and continues to shape how communities respond to research recruitment today.

The U.S. Public Health Service Syphilis Study at Tuskegee (1932-1972) enrolled 399 Black men with syphilis and 201 uninfected controls, promising free medical care and burial insurance while deliberately withholding treatment — including penicillin after it became the standard of care in 1947 — to study the natural progression of untreated syphilis. The study ended only when a whistleblower leaked details to the press. Its legacy is a documented, rational distrust of biomedical research and institutions among many Black Americans.

The story of Henrietta Lacks and the HeLa cell line adds another dimension. Lacks was a Black woman whose cervical cancer cells were taken without her knowledge or consent at Johns Hopkins Hospital in 1951. Her cells — known as HeLa cells — became the first human cell line that could be kept alive and grown in the laboratory indefinitely. They have been used in thousands of scientific studies and generated billions of dollars in commercial value. The Lacks family received no compensation and was not informed for decades.

These histories matter for precision medicine recruitment because trust is the prerequisite for participation. When researchers approach Black, Indigenous, or other historically exploited communities with genomic research offers, they are entering those conversations carrying this institutional history — whether or not individual researchers know it or intend it. Effective, ethical recruitment requires community engagement, transparent data governance, and demonstrated benefit to the communities being recruited.

body.analogy: Imagine a bank that, for decades, systematically overcharged customers from a particular neighborhood, denied them loans based on their address, and never faced consequences. Now the bank has new leadership, new policies, and genuinely wants to serve that neighborhood. But residents remember — or their parents remember — and they are not wrong to be cautious. The bank's new good intentions do not erase the institutional memory of harm.
body.bridge: Research institutions that previously exploited communities of color now seek to recruit those communities into genomic research for what they believe are legitimate scientific and equity goals. The skepticism these communities exhibit is not irrational — it is a rational protective response to documented institutional harm. Building trust requires time, transparency, community control over data, and demonstrated reciprocal benefit.
body.concept: Why historical research exploitation creates present-day trust deficits

children.text: Indigenous Data Sovereignty and the CARE Principles

Indigenous communities face a distinct set of concerns around genomic research. Beyond the shared history of exploitation that many minority communities experience, Indigenous peoples have specific legal and political status as sovereign nations, with implications for how data about their members is collected, stored, shared, and used.

Indigenous data sovereignty is the right of Indigenous peoples to govern the collection, ownership, and application of data about their communities. The CARE Principles for Indigenous Data Governance — Collective Benefit, Authority to Control, Responsibility, and Ethics — provide a framework for how genomic research involving Indigenous communities should be structured. These principles assert that data about Indigenous peoples belongs to and should serve Indigenous peoples, not external researchers or corporations.

Specific cases have illustrated the stakes. The Havasupai Tribe of Arizona participated in a diabetes genetics study at Arizona State University in the 1990s, donating blood samples for that specific purpose. Researchers then used the samples for other studies — including research on schizophrenia, population migration, and inbreeding — without tribal consent. The Havasupai sued, eventually settling in 2010, and the case has since been a touchstone for discussions of Indigenous research ethics.

In Vermont, the Abenaki Nation — Vermont's only state-recognized Indigenous nation — has its own community priorities and sensitivities around research and data governance. Any genomic research initiative seeking to include Abenaki community members must engage tribal leadership as partners, not merely as a recruitment population, and must respect the community's authority to decide whether and on what terms genomic research is appropriate.
LGBTQ+ Populations and Genomic Research Gaps

LGBTQ+ populations — lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer, and other sexual and gender minority (SGM) individuals — represent another group systematically underrepresented in genomic and biomedical research. This is partly a data collection problem: most electronic health records and research databases have not systematically collected sexual orientation or gender identity (SOGI) data, making it impossible to study health disparities that may have genetic or gene-environment interaction components.

LGBTQ+ individuals also have documented higher rates of several conditions with potential genomic components — including depression, anxiety, substance use disorders, and certain cancers — but the research to disentangle genetic from social and minority stress contributions to these disparities is in its infancy. The NIH Sexual & Gender Minority Research Office and the All of Us program's explicit SGM inclusion goals are beginning to address this gap.
Rural Populations and Precision Medicine Access Barriers

Rural populations face a distinct set of precision medicine access barriers that are structural rather than cultural. These include geographic distance from specialized genetic services, limited broadband access needed for telegenetics, provider shortages that mean primary care physicians have little time to engage with genomic complexity, and insurance gaps that make high-cost genomic testing and targeted therapies financially inaccessible.

Rural patients with cancer have historically had less access to tumor genomic profiling — the first step in precision oncology — because testing and molecular expertise concentrate in academic centers. Programs that bring testing to community practices can close that gap: a 2024 study in JNCI Cancer Spectrum of 1,258 patients in the Maine Cancer Genomics Initiative, which deployed tumor testing through community and rural oncology practices, found that rurality was not associated with receipt of genome-matched treatment. Access, not geography itself, is the barrier.

body.title: Rural and Structural Access Gaps in Precision Medicine

children.text: Vermont-Specific Equity Challenges: Refugee Populations and Rural Geography

Vermont is among the whitest states in the nation by percentage, but it hosts a significant and growing refugee population — particularly in Burlington and surrounding communities — that represents extraordinary genetic and ancestral diversity. Vermont has resettled refugees from Bhutan, Somalia, Democratic Republic of Congo, Bosnia, Sudan, and dozens of other countries.

For refugee populations, precision medicine access barriers multiply. Language barriers complicate genetic counseling, which is inherently nuanced and requires precise communication about probability, uncertainty, and family implications. Reference databases have almost no data from many refugee-origin populations, increasing VUS rates dramatically. Cultural frameworks around fate, family disclosure, and heredity may differ significantly from those embedded in standard genetic counseling practice.

Genetic counselors working with Vermont's refugee communities need cultural competence, access to professional medical interpreters (not family members, who may selectively filter difficult information), and awareness that the Western individualistic framework for genetic decision-making — emphasizing personal autonomy and individual disclosure choices — may not fit the community-oriented decision-making frameworks of many refugee cultures.

body.body: UVMMC's Global Health Program and its associated refugee health clinic provide primary care to Burlington's refugee communities. The program has developed culturally adapted health communication approaches and works with community health workers who share cultural and linguistic backgrounds with patient populations. As genomic medicine becomes more integrated into primary care, these established community relationships represent a critical infrastructure for equitable genomic service delivery.
body.outcome: The Global Health Program model — community health workers as cultural bridges, professional interpreter use, and community engagement in service design — represents a replicable approach for extending precision medicine services to linguistically and culturally diverse populations in rural states.
body.source: UVMMC Global Health Program; Vermont Refugee Health Program Annual Reports
body.title: University of Vermont Medical Center Global Health Program

children.text: What Equitable Precision Medicine Actually Requires

Equitable precision medicine is not simply a matter of increasing diversity in research databases, though that is essential. It requires changes at multiple levels — research design, clinical service delivery, technology development, insurance policy, and community trust-building — working simultaneously.

steps.description: Genomic databases, GWAS studies, and variant interpretation tools must include sufficient representation from all major ancestry groups to ensure that polygenic risk scores and variant classifications are valid across populations — not just European ancestry individuals.
steps.title: Diverse, representative research databases

steps.description: Underrepresented communities must be partners in research design, not merely recruitment targets. This means tribal consultation for Indigenous communities, community advisory boards for other groups, and genuine power-sharing over data governance and benefit distribution.
steps.title: Community-engaged research design

steps.description: Genomic testing and precision medicine therapies must be covered by Medicaid and other public payers at rates that ensure access regardless of income. Inconsistent Medicaid coverage for tumor profiling, targeted therapies, and genetic counseling is a structural equity failure.
steps.title: Insurance coverage and payment reform

steps.description: The genetic counseling workforce must expand dramatically, and telegenetics must be fully reimbursed to extend services to rural areas. Community health workers trained in genomic health communication can extend the reach of genetic counselors in underserved communities.
steps.title: Workforce expansion and telegenetics

steps.description: Genetic counseling and genomic health communication must be available in the languages spoken by patients, with cultural adaptation for communities whose frameworks for understanding heredity, family, and risk differ from the Western individualistic model embedded in standard practice.
steps.title: Culturally and linguistically adapted services

body.title: What Equitable Precision Medicine Requires: A Framework

children.text: The equity failures in precision medicine are not primarily failures of individual prejudice — they are failures of system design. Genomic databases were built with the researchers available, which happened to be primarily from European ancestry academic institutions. Fixing this requires intentional redesign of research infrastructure, not just increased awareness.

body.misconception: The solution to genomic inequity is simply to recruit more diverse participants into existing research frameworks.
body.reality: Recruiting diverse participants into research systems that were not designed with their interests, governance preferences, or data sovereignty in mind replicates historical exploitation in a new form. Equitable genomic research requires restructuring how data governance works — giving communities authority over their data, ensuring benefit flows back to participating communities, and building infrastructure that serves underrepresented populations rather than merely extracting data from them.

body.answer: VUS findings are more common in patients of African ancestry because the databases used to classify variants — such as ClinVar — have been built predominantly from research on European ancestry populations. A variant that has been observed many times in European ancestry individuals may be well-classified as benign or pathogenic; a variant that appears primarily in African ancestry individuals may lack sufficient reference data for classification, resulting in VUS status. This is a limitation of the database, not a feature of the patient's biology. The provider should: (1) explain clearly that VUS does not mean dangerous and is not a basis for preventive surgery; (2) refer to a board-certified genetic counselor for comprehensive counseling; (3) encourage the patient's relatives to be tested, as additional family data can help reclassify variants; (4) inform the patient that VUS classifications are frequently updated as databases improve, and her lab should re-analyze her variants over time; and (5) acknowledge that the higher VUS rate in patients of African ancestry is a systemic inequity in the genomic research infrastructure, not a personal or biological characteristic.
body.hint: Think about what drives VUS classification and how variant databases are constructed.
body.question: A Black woman in Vermont receives BRCA1/2 testing through her OB/GYN after a family history of breast cancer. Her result shows three variants of uncertain significance (VUS). She is devastated and asks whether she should have a prophylactic mastectomy. What should her provider understand about why VUS findings are more common in patients of African ancestry, and how should this be communicated?

body.answer: The CARE Principles require: Collective Benefit — the research must generate direct benefit to the Abenaki community, not just academic publications or commercial applications that flow back to the research institution; Authority to Control — the Abenaki Nation must have genuine authority over how their members' data is collected, stored, analyzed, and shared, including veto power over secondary uses; Responsibility — researchers have an ongoing obligation to the community that extends beyond the data collection period; and Ethics — research must be consistent with the community's own values and governance processes. In practice, a genuine data sovereignty approach would: involve tribal leadership as co-investigators with intellectual property rights, not just as a community advisory board; require that data be stored in systems the tribe controls; require explicit consent for every new use case rather than blanket consent; specify that data cannot be shared with commercial genomics companies; guarantee that research results and benefits flow back to the community; and include community health workers as co-researchers who will remain in the community after the study ends. The Havasupai case specifically teaches that researchers must obtain specific consent for each study use — blanket consent for 'diabetes research' does not authorize use of samples for ancestry, migration, or psychiatric studies.
body.hint: Think about what CARE stands for and what the Havasupai case taught the field about scope of consent.
body.question: A Vermont health system wants to partner with the Western Abenaki community to study genetic factors in type 2 diabetes, which affects the community at elevated rates. Community members have expressed interest in the health question but concern about how their genetic data will be used. What does the CARE framework require of researchers in this situation, and what would a genuine data sovereignty approach look like?

points: More than 78% of GWAS participants have been of European ancestry, making precision medicine less scientifically valid for the 84% of the global population that is not of European ancestry — this is a scientific accuracy problem, not just an ethical concern.

Polygenic risk scores trained on European data perform substantially worse in non-European populations, meaning clinical decisions based on these scores are systematically less accurate for patients of African, Asian, Indigenous, and other non-European ancestry.

Higher rates of variants of uncertain significance in non-European BRCA testing reflect database inadequacy, not biological ambiguity — variant classification databases are built from skewed reference populations.

The Tuskegee syphilis study and the Henrietta Lacks/HeLa cell case are not historical curiosities — they established patterns of research exploitation whose legacy shapes community participation in genomic research today.

Indigenous data sovereignty and the CARE principles (Collective Benefit, Authority to Control, Responsibility, Ethics) require that research involving Indigenous communities be governed by those communities, not by external institutions.

Economic barriers — inconsistent Medicaid coverage for tumor profiling, targeted therapies, and genetic counseling — mean that precision medicine's benefits are currently distributed along income lines.

Vermont's refugee communities face compounded barriers to genomic equity: language barriers in genetic counseling, near-complete absence of their ancestries in reference databases, and cultural frameworks that differ from the individualistic model embedded in standard genetic counseling.

Equitable precision medicine requires redesigning research infrastructure, not merely recruiting more diverse participants — communities must have authority over their data and receive direct benefit from research participation.
body.title: Module 6 Key Takeaways

learningObjectives: Explain why the lack of diversity in genomic databases is a scientific validity problem, not just an ethical concern
Describe how polygenic risk scores perform differently across ancestry groups and why this matters clinically
Identify the historical events that created legitimate distrust of genomic research among marginalized communities
Explain the principles of indigenous data sovereignty and the CARE principles
Describe what the NIH All of Us program is attempting to accomplish and its key design choices
Identify the economic, geographic, and structural barriers that limit precision medicine access for Vermont's underserved populations
summary: Precision medicine's promise is undermined by a fundamental problem: the genomic databases and research studies that power it are built overwhelmingly from people of European ancestry. This is not just an ethical concern — it is a scientific validity problem that produces less accurate polygenic risk scores, higher rates of ambiguous genetic findings, and systematically worse care for non-European patients. This module examines the structural causes of genomic inequity, the historical trauma that makes diverse participation in research difficult, and what equitable precision medicine actually requires — including Vermont-specific challenges around refugee populations, Abenaki communities, and rural access.
title: The Diversity Deficit: Why Precision Medicine Must Work for Everyone
